alignment.note: Greek ὁμοίως and Latin Similiter are simple adverbs ('likewise'); the Syriac ܘܗܟܢܐ prefixes the conjunctive waw ('and thus'), folding the connective δέ/et into a single demonstrative-adverbial form rather than rendering it as a separate particle.

The Greek transitional particle δέ ('now/but') has no discrete counterpart in either the Vulgate or the Peshitta; the Vulgate et and the Syriac ܐܦ render only the adjunctive καί, leaving the postpositive δέ unrepresented.
οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς / ܪܒܝ ܟܗܢܐ / summi sacerdotes

Greek ἐμπαίζοντες and Latin illudentes are single present participles; the Syriac expresses the durative aspect periphrastically with the active participle ܓܚܟܝܢ plus the auxiliary ܗܘܘ ('were mocking'), a standard Syriac construction for continuous past action.

Greek πρὸς ἀλλήλους and Latin ad alterutrum use a reciprocal pronoun ('to one another'); the Syriac renders the reciprocity idiomatically as ܚܕ ܥܡ ܚܕ ('one with one'), distributing the sense across three tokens rather than a single pronoun.

Greek μετὰ τῶν γραμματέων and Latin cum scribis use a preposition plus noun ('with the scribes'); the Syriac ܘܣܦܪܐ employs only the conjunctive waw prefixed to 'scribes' ('and the scribes'), coordinating rather than subordinating the scribes to the chief priests.

Greek ἔλεγον (imperfect) and Latin dicebant render the durative 'were saying'; the Syriac ܘܐܡܪܝܢ uses the participle with prefixed waw. The Vulgate's colon (token 10) marks the onset of direct speech, a punctuational feature absent as a discrete token in the Greek and Syriac.

Greek ἄλλους ἔσωσεν and Latin alios salvos fecit ('others he saved/made safe') employ the verb of salvation; the Syriac ܐܚܪܢܐ ܐܚܝ uses the root kh-y-a 'to give life/quicken', a lexical choice that frames deliverance as life-giving rather than rescue, consistent with Syriac usage for σῴζω.

Greek δύναται and Latin potest both denote ability ('he is able'); the Syriac ܡܫܟܚ derives from the root sh-k-kh ('to find/be able'), the regular Syriac verb for capacity, a cognate-but-distinct lexical choice for the modal sense.

Greek σῶσαι (aorist infinitive 'to save') is matched by the Syriac infinitive ܠܡܚܝܘ ('to give life', root kh-y-a) and the Latin periphrastic salvum facere ('to make safe'). The Vulgate's preceding semicolon (token 14) punctuates the antithesis between the two clauses.
